en: The Bodhisattva Śīla-sūtra, extracted from the "Bodhisattvabhūmi" within the "Maulī Bhūmi" of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
spoken by Maitreya Bodhisattva;
translated by the Śramaṇa Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

If bodhisattvas have already received the pure precepts undertaken by bodhisattvas, they should repeatedly and with focused attention reflect for themselves: "This is what a bodhisattva ought to do; this is not what a bodhisattva ought to do."
Having reflected thus, one should then diligently train in order to accomplish the activities that are rightly performed.

Furthermore, one should apply oneself with single-minded diligence to hearing the Bodhisattva Sūtrapiṭaka and the Bodhisattva Mātṛkā; according to what has been heard, one should diligently train therein.
If bodhisattvas abide in the ethical discipline of restraint, there are four types of dharmas that constitute defeats. What are these four?
If a bodhisattva, out of a desire for gain and honor, praises themselves and disparages others, this is called the first dharma of defeat.

If bodhisattvas currently possess wealth and resources, yet due to their nature of stinginess regarding wealth, they do not give rise to compassion or practice generous relinquishment when those who are suffering, impoverished, and without refuge or protector come before them seeking wealth.

When one who is correctly seeking the Dharma comes before them, because they are by nature stingy regarding the Dharma, they do not relinquish or bestow it even though they currently possess it; this is called the second *pārājika* offense.

If bodhisattvas nurture such a form of the obsession with anger, they do not stop merely at initiating harsh speech; because they are obscured by anger, they further use their hands, feet, clods of earth, stones, swords, or staves to strike, injure, and afflict sentient beings, harboring within a fierce and intense intention of resentment and committing transgressions.
If he comes to offer counsel and apology, yet the bodhisattva does not accept it, does not endure it, and does not relinquish his grudge, this is called the third *parājika* offense.

If a bodhisattva slanders the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and out of a fondness for proclaiming, revealing, and establishing counterfeit teachings, either personally believes in or follows such counterfeit teachings, this is called the fourth *parājika* offense.

If a bodhisattva commits even one of these four defeats (*pārājika*), let alone all of them, they will no longer be capable, within this present life, of increasing and gathering the vast provisions for enlightenment; nor will they be capable, within this present life, of purifying their resolve.
Such a person is called a semblance bodhisattva, not a true bodhisattva.
If a bodhisattva commits the four types of defeats through weak or middling grades of entanglements, they do not forfeit their bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline.
An offense committed with superior-grade entanglement is termed "abandonment.
If a bodhisattva repeatedly commits any of the four defeats (*pārājika*), acting without any sense of shame or remorse,
and even developing a deep fondness for them while perceiving them as meritorious, it should be known that this is called an offense with superior-grade entanglement.

It is not the case that a bodhisattva loses the bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline by merely once manifesting an offense involving defeat (*pārājika*), as it is for a bhikṣu who, upon committing an offense involving defeat, immediately abandons the prātimokṣa vows.
If, through such a transgression, a bodhisattva abandons the bodhisattva vow of pure ethical discipline, they are capable of receiving it again within this very life; they are not incapable.
Just as a bhikṣu who dwells in the prātimokṣa vows, having committed a pārājika offense, is incapable of receiving them again in this present life;

so too, a bodhisattva dwelling in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline (śīla-saṃvara) should understand whether there has been a transgression or not, whether it is defiled or undefiled, and whether it is of weak, medium, or superior degree.
If bodhisattvas, abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, do not daily make offerings—whether small or great—to the Tathāgata, or to a *caitya* built for the Tathāgata;
or to the True Dharma, or to a scripture written for the True Dharma, namely the Bodhisattva *Sūtrapiṭaka* and *Mātṛkā*;

or to the Saṃgha, namely the assembly of bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions who have entered the great stages; at the very least by prostrating once with their body, or at the very least by praising with a single four-line verse the true virtues of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha; [they incur an offense].
If one fails to recollect the true merits of the Triple Gem with even a single moment of pure faith,
thereby allowing days and nights to pass in vain, this is called an offense and a transgression.
If one commits a transgression due to a lack of respect, indolence, or laziness, it is an afflicted transgression.
If one commits a transgression through a lapse of mindfulness, it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
namely, when the mind is deranged;
or, if one has already entered the stage of pure intention (*śuddhāśayabhūmi*), there is always no transgression.

Just as a bhikṣu who has attained verified clarity (*avetyaprasāda*) naturally and at all times serves and makes offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha with superior requisites, so too does a bodhisattva who has attained pure intention.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, possesses great desire and lacks contentment, and gives rise to attachment toward gains and honors without relinquishing them, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation.
There is no transgression in the following case:

when one has generated the desire to abandon those [defilements], exerts diligent effort, and applies the remedies; yet, despite striving to suppress them, one is obscured by intense innate afflictions such that they frequently manifest.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, sees elders, those of virtuous merit worthy of respect, or fellow practitioners of the Dharma arrive, yet—being constrained by arrogance and harboring a mind of resentment or a mind of malice—fails to rise to greet them and fails to offer them a superior seat.

If others come to converse, offer greetings, or inquire after one, and being constrained by pride, harboring resentment, or harboring anger and vexation, one responds with words that do not accord with correct principle, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation.

It is not due to arrogance, nor is it with a mind of resentment or malice; rather, it arises solely from laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, and a neutral state of mind. This is called an offense and a transgression, yet it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
namely, when one is afflicted by a serious illness;
or when the mind is deranged.
Either while one is asleep, another person, having conceived the thought that one is awake, approaches and engages in conversation, offers greetings and consolation, or puts questions;
or while one is oneself expounding the various dharmas, discussing their meaning, or making definitive judgments;
or again, while one is conversing with others and offering greetings and consolation.
Or he listens attentively while others discourse on the Dharma or engage in the definitive analysis of its meaning;
or, when there is someone who transgresses against those who preach the True Dharma, he acts out of a desire to protect the mind of that preacher;
or he desires to employ skillful means to discipline and subdue them, leading them away from unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states.
There is no offense if one protects the monastic regulations; or if one does not respond in order to protect the minds of many sentient beings.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, is invited by another to go to a private home or another monastery to accept offerings of food, drink, clothing, or other requisites of life, yet—being constrained by pride, harboring resentment, or harboring anger—does not go to that place nor accepts the invitation, this is called an offense, a transgression, and is a defiled offense.

If, due to indolence, laziness, forgetfulness, or a neutral state of mind, one does not go to that place or accept the invitation, this is called an offense and a transgression; it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if one is afflicted by illness;
or if one lacks physical strength;
Either the mind is deranged;
or the location is remote;
or the path is dangerous.
Or, wishing to employ skillful means to discipline and subdue them, leading them out of unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states;
or because they have been previously invited by others;
or for the sake of uninterrupted cultivation of all wholesome dharmas, desiring to protect the category of virtue so that it is not abandoned even for a moment.
Either for the purpose of attracting and gathering hitherto unknown meanings,
or for the purpose of ensuring that the meaning of the Dharma one has heard does not decline;

and just as it is for the purpose of ensuring that the meaning of the Dharma one has heard does not decline, one should know that the same applies to the definitive resolution of doctrinal discussions (*arthaviniścaya*).
Alternatively, one may know that the other person harbors a malicious intent and has come to invite [one] under false pretenses;
or one may do so to protect another from excessive resentment;
or to uphold the monastic regulations.
If one does not go to their location or accept their invitation, there is no transgression in either case.

However, if a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, refuses and does not accept when others offer various kinds of precious materials—such as raw gold, dyed cloth, *maṇi* gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, and so forth—as well as various other excellent and superior material gifts and offerings, out of a mind of resentment or anger, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted offense because it involves abandoning sentient beings.

If, due to indolence, laziness, forgetfulness, or a neutral state of mind, one rejects and does not accept [the teaching], this is called an offense; it is a transgression, yet it is not a defiled violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases: if the mind is deranged;
or if, having experienced a sensation, the mind gives rise to attachment.
Or one observes that at a later time he will certainly regret it;
or one knows that he is confused regarding the act of giving;
or one knows that the donor gives away as soon as they receive [the gift].
By reason of these causes and conditions, one will certainly become impoverished;
or one knows that this object belongs to the Saṃgha or to a stūpa;
or one knows that this object was obtained through robbery or theft from another.
Or, if one knows that because of these causes and conditions the object will give rise to many faults and afflictions—
such as being killed, bound, punished, or dismissed, or being censured or rebuked— and thus refuses to accept it, there is no transgression in any of these cases.

If a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, refuses to bestow the Dharma upon another who comes seeking it out of a mind of resentment, a mind of malice, or a mind corrupted by envy, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
If, due to indolence, laziness, forgetfulness, or a neutral state of mind, one does not bestow the Dharma, this is called an offense and a transgression; however, it is not a defiled violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
when non-Buddhists seek out faults and shortcomings;
or when one is suffering from a serious illness.
Either his mind is deranged;
or he desires to employ skillful means to discipline and subdue them, leading them out of unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states;
or he has not yet thoroughly mastered these teachings.
Or perhaps he sees that they lack reverence and have no sense of shame, coming to listen and receive the teaching with improper deportment;

or he knows that they are of dull faculties, who, upon encountering the vast teachings of the Dharma, would become deeply terrified, give rise to false views, increase their perverse attachments, and suffer decline, ruin, and affliction;
or he knows that once the Dharma reaches their hands, they will disseminate it to those who are unworthy.
If one does not bestow [gifts] upon them, there is no transgression in any case.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice toward sentient beings who are violent and immoral, and—motivated by those very beings' violence and immorality—employs means to abandon them and fails to provide benefit, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled offense.
If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, or due to forgetfulness, one fails to act for the benefit [of others], this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a non-afflicted violation.

Why is this? It is not that Bodhisattvas give rise to a mind of compassion toward those sentient beings who maintain pure ethical discipline in their physical, verbal, and mental actions and whose conduct is tranquil, with the desire to benefit them.
There is no transgression when, regarding sentient beings who are violent and immoral and who manifest in various causes of suffering,
one’s mind is deranged.
Or it may be that he wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them, as explained in detail previously;
or it may be for the sake of protecting the minds of many sentient beings;
or it may be to uphold the regulations of the Saṃgha.
There is no transgression if one intentionally abandons [an action] and does not provide benefit.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dwells in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), just as the Bhagavān established prohibitive offenses (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) within the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya* for the sake of protecting others—restraining the śrāvakas from committing them so that sentient beings who have not yet gained pure faith may develop it, and those who already possess pure faith may cause it to increase further.
In this regard, Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas should train equally, without distinction. Why is this?

Because even Śrāvakas, who prioritize their own self-interest, do not abandon the practice of protecting others; they train in the points of training so that sentient beings who have no faith may gain it, and those who already have faith may increase it—how much more so for Bodhisattvas, who prioritize the benefit of others?

If bodhisattvas abide in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, they should not train in the same manner as śrāvakas regarding those prohibited offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) which the Bhagavān established in the *Prātimokṣa-vinaya* to cause śrāvakas to dwell with few concerns, few activities, and few aspirations, thereby restraining them from committing such acts;
in these matters, the bodhisattva and the śrāvaka should not study equally.

Why is this? Because for the śrāvakas, who regard self-benefit as supreme and disregard the benefit of others, it may be called "excellent" to dwell with few affairs, few activities, and few aspirations regarding the benefit of others;

however, for bodhisattvas, who regard the benefit of others as supreme and disregard self-benefit, it cannot be called "excellent" to dwell with few affairs, few activities, and few aspirations regarding the benefit of others.

In this way, for the sake of benefiting others, a bodhisattva should seek hundreds of thousands of various kinds of robes from non-relatives—such as elders, householders, brahmins, and those who give freely—and having observed whether those sentient beings have the means or not, he should accept what is given according to their capacity. As it is said regarding the seeking of robes, the same applies to the seeking of alms bowls.
Just as one seeks robes and alms bowls, so too may one seek various kinds of silk threads oneself and have those who are not relatives weave them into robes for one.

For the sake of benefiting others, one should store various *kauseya* (silk) garments and various sitting and bedding utensils, each up to a hundred; one may also take and accumulate dyed fabrics of precious colors numbering in the hundreds of thousands of *koṭis*, even exceeding that number.

Among such cases as these, regarding those minor matters, minor activities, and minor aspirations for which one dwells in restraint and prohibition of transgressions, a bodhisattva does not train together with the śrāvakas.

If a bodhisattva dwelling in the code of pure ethical discipline, while engaged in the benefit of others, harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice and dwells in minor matters, minor activities, and minor aspirations, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.

If, due to laziness, indolence, forgetfulness, or a neutral state of mind, one dwells with few concerns, few activities, and few aspirations, this is called an offense and a transgression; however, it is not a defiled offense.

If bodhisattvas, dwelling securely in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, through skillful means and for the sake of benefiting others, should occasionally engage in certain natural misdeeds (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), they do not thereby commit a transgression against the bodhisattva precepts; rather, by reason of this, they generate great merit.

This refers, for example, to a bodhisattva who sees an evil bandit who, out of greed for wealth, intends to kill many living beings, or intends to harm a noble śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or bodhisattva, or intends to commit many acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma).
Having seen this, he reflected: "If I were to take the life of that evil person, I would fall into hell;

yet if I do not take his life, the karma of an immediate retribution will be completed and he shall suffer great agony. It would be better for me to kill him and fall into hell than to allow him to undergo the suffering of an immediate retribution."

Thus, with such an intention and reflection, the bodhisattva—whether with a virtuous mind or an indeterminate mind—recognizes this matter regarding those sentient beings; for the sake of the future, he gives rise to profound shame and remorse, and with a heart of compassion, he takes their life.
By reason of these causes and conditions, one does not commit any transgression against the bodhisattva precepts and generates much merit.

Furthermore, suppose a bodhisattva sees a superior official or a high-ranking minister who is extremely violent and cruel, lacking any compassion for sentient beings, and who specializes in oppressing and harassing them.

Having seen this, the bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of compassion and develops the intention to bring about benefit and happiness; then, according to his capacity, he either dismisses or degrades them from their positions of superior rank.
By reason of these causes and conditions, one does not commit any transgression against the bodhisattva precepts and generates great merit.

Furthermore, suppose a bodhisattva sees a bandit or thief who has plundered another’s property—whether it be the belongings of the Saṃgha or the property of a stūpa—and having taken a great deal of such goods, claims them as his own and uses them according to his own pleasure.

Having seen this, the bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of compassion and develops the intention to bring benefit and happiness to those sentient beings. To the extent of his ability, he forcibly takes away [the property], so that they shall not enjoy such wealth and thereby suffer for a long night of meaninglessness and disadvantage. By reason of this, the seized treasures and goods are restored: if they belong to the Saṃgha, they are returned to the Saṃgha; if they belong to a stūpa, they are returned to the stūpa; and if they belong to sentient beings, they are returned to those sentient beings.

Furthermore, I see sentient beings, such as garden owners, who take property belonging to the Saṃgha or property belonging to a stūpa, claiming it as their own and using it according to their own desires.

Having seen this, the bodhisattva reflects upon that evil and gives rise to a mind of compassion, thinking: "May they not, because of this karma of improper enjoyment, undergo long nights of meaninglessness and disadvantage. Accordingly, to the best of his ability, he causes them to relinquish what they control.
In this way, although the bodhisattva takes what is not given, there is no transgression, and much merit is generated.

Furthermore, suppose a bodhisattva living as a householder sees a woman who is currently unattached and practicing sexual conduct, who sets her mind upon the bodhisattva and seeks non-celibate behavior.

Having seen this, the bodhisattva reflects with focused attention: "I must not allow my mind to become resentful, for that would produce much demerit. If I comply with his wishes, he will attain mastery; through skillful means, I shall establish him in peace, cause him to plant roots of merit, and also lead him to abandon unwholesome karma."
If one dwells in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion yet engages in unchaste conduct,
although one practices such defiled dharmas, there is no transgression and much merit is generated.
However, an ordained bodhisattva, in order to protect the instructions of the noble śrāvakas so that they are not destroyed or extinguished, must under no circumstances engage in unchaste conduct.

Furthermore, for example, when there are many sentient beings facing the perils of losing their lives, imprisonment and bondage, the amputation of hands or feet, or the cutting off of the nose, the cutting off of the ears, or the gouging out of the eyes, although a bodhisattva would never knowingly speak a falsehood even at the cost of his own life, he may nevertheless speak a falsehood after deliberate reflection for the sake of rescuing and liberating those sentient beings.

In brief, when a bodhisattva considers only the welfare of sentient beings and not their lack of welfare, and speaks contrary words while concealing his thoughts with correct awareness—doing so solely for the benefit of all sentient beings and without any defiled mind—he commits no transgression against the bodhisattva precepts and generates great merit.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who have been taken under the influence of evil companions and feel such affection for them that they cannot abandon them, the bodhisattva gives rise to a heart of compassion and develops the intention to bring them benefit and happiness.

To the best of his ability and strength, he speaks words of separation so as to cause them to distance themselves from those evil companions and relinquish their mutual intimacy, lest these sentient beings, by remaining close to evil companions, undergo long nights of meaninglessness and disadvantage.

In this way, when a bodhisattva speaks words that cause division with a mind intent on benefiting others, thereby alienating those who are in love, there is no transgression; rather, much merit is generated.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings traveling along a wrong path or acting unrighteously, he utters harsh and severe words to sternly rebuke them, employing skillful means to lead them out of unwholesome states and establish them in wholesome ones.
In this way, when a bodhisattva, with a mind intent on benefiting others, utters harsh words toward sentient beings, there is no transgression; rather, much merit is generated.

Furthermore, suppose a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who take pleasure in performing arts, chanting, and singing, or who take pleasure in meaningless discourse concerning kings, thieves, food and drink, lewdness, and the streets.

The Bodhisattva is skillful in all these matters; toward those sentient beings, he gives rise to a mind of compassion and generates the intention for their benefit and happiness. He manifests various performances associated with frivolous speech—such as singing, chanting, and recitation, as well as discourses on kings, thieves, food and drink, and the ways of lust—to delight and attract those beings, bringing them under his influence. Through such skillful means, he guides and leads them out of unwholesome states and establishes them in wholesome ones.
When a bodhisattva thus engages in frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*), there is no transgression, and much merit is generated.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), gives rise to deceit, hollow talk, and the display of signs; seeks profit through profit by means of artifice and investigation; and relishes the dharma of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*) without shame, persisting in it and refusing to abandon it—this is called an offense, a transgression, and is a defiled violation.
There is no transgression if,
while striving with diligence to eliminate [the afflictions] that have arisen, one's afflictions are so intense that they overwhelm the mind and manifest from time to time.

If a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, is moved by agitation such that the mind is not tranquil, does not delight in tranquility, engages in loud play, clamor, and chatter, or acts with frivolity and leaping about, seeking to provoke laughter in others—due to such conditions, this is called an offense, a transgression, and it is an afflicted violation.
If it arises due to a lapse of mindfulness, it is not a defiled transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if it arises for the purpose of dispelling [the affliction], as explained in detail previously; and so forth.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to resolve the resentment others have conceived so that it may cease;
if one wishes to dispel the sorrow and affliction others have conceived;
or if others are naturally inclined toward the aforementioned matters, one employs skillful means to embrace them, honoring their wishes, protecting them, and acting in accordance with them.

If other sentient beings harbor suspicion and obstruction toward a bodhisattva, inwardly concealing malice, hatred, and malicious schemes while outwardly manifesting a joyful countenance to represent inner purity;
in all such cases as these, there is no transgression.
If any bodhisattvas, while dwelling in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, give rise to such a view and establish such a doctrine as this:
"A bodhisattva should not rejoice in nirvana, but should instead feel aversion toward and turn away from nirvana;

one should not fear the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), nor seek their total eradication, nor should one single-mindedly give rise to a mind of weary detachment [from cyclic existence]; [they commit a transgression].

If one were to say that Bodhisattvas wander through birth and death for three incalculable eons seeking great enlightenment [as if it were merely a matter of time], this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
Why is this? Just as the śrāvakas delight in and draw near to their own nirvāṇa, and feel deep-seated revulsion toward all afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),

so too does the bodhisattva delight in and draw near to great parinirvāṇa, and feel deep-seated revulsion toward all afflictions and secondary afflictions— exceeding that of the former by hundreds of thousands of koṭis.
Because the śrāvakas apply themselves to correct practice solely for the sake of attaining benefit for their own single person,
whereas the bodhisattvas apply themselves to correct practice for the sake of all sentient beings universally attaining benefit.

Therefore, a bodhisattva should diligently cultivate and gather an undefiled mind; while engaging in accordance with contaminated phenomena, they shall achieve a state that surpasses the undefiled dharmas of all arhats.

If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, do not protect against or clear away untrustworthy words uttered about themselves—namely, evil reports, ill repute, or bad fame.
If the matter is true and one does not avoid or protect [against it], this is called an offense; there is a transgression, and it is an afflicted offense.
If the matter is not true and one does not clear oneself of it, this is called an offense; there is a transgression, but it is a non-afflicted offense.
There is no offense if it is another non-Buddhist,
or if the other person is full of hatred and jealousy.
If, having gone forth for oneself, one incurs a reputation for slander due to the practice of begging or the cultivation of wholesome deeds;
or if one is obscured by anger;
or if one’s mind is inverted.
If slanderous reports are spread, there is no transgression whatsoever.

If a bodhisattva, dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, sees sentient beings who could obtain benefit through various harsh applications or intense applications, yet refrains from acting out of a desire to protect them from distress;
this is called an offense, a transgression, but it is not a defiled offense.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if, by considering the circumstances, one perceives that it would result in little benefit in this present life and much mental distress;
or if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, returns abuse for abuse received from another.
When others respond with anger, he responds with anger;
when others strike him, he strikes back;
when others mock him, he mocks them in return.
This is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, commits an offense against another sentient being;
or if he does not commit it himself, yet the other suspects him of having committed an offense;
If, out of a mind of resentment and jealousy, or due to being gripped by pride, one fails to apologize properly and instead treats the other with neglect and disdain;
this is called an offense, a transgression, and is a defiled violation.

If, due to laziness, indolence, negligence, or a lack of gratitude and a tendency toward dismissal, one fails to do so, this is called an offense and a transgression; however, it is not a defiled violation.
There is no transgression if one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them, leading them from unwholesome states and establishing them in wholesome states;
or if they are followers of non-Buddhist paths.
If one expects that the other will only accept the apology after one has first committed an unrighteous and culpable act;
or if that sentient being is by nature prone to contention and their anger would increase manifold upon receiving the apology;
or if one knows that the other is by nature patient and devoid of resentment; [in these cases, one should not offer an apology].
If one knows for certain that the other person has apologized for the offense and feels deep shame, yet does not accept the apology and repentance, there is no transgression in any case.

However, if a bodhisattva dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline is offended by another who subsequently repents and apologizes in accordance with the Dharma and with equanimity, yet—driven by a mind of resentment and wishing to harm or vex them—does not accept the apology, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted transgression.

Although one harbors no feelings of resentment toward them and has no desire to cause them harm or distress, because of an innate disposition that lacks forbearance, one does not accept their apology; this is also termed an offense and a transgression, yet it is not a defiled violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue that person—details of which should all be understood as previously explained;
or if one does not accept an apology because it was offered in a manner that is contrary to the Dharma or inequitable, there is likewise no transgression.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline, harbors anger toward others, maintains it continuously, and does not relinquish it once it has arisen, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted offense.
There is no transgression if, for the sake of abandoning that [fault], one generates the desire to do so, as explained in detail previously.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), out of the excessive power of attachment to being served and with a mind of craving, manages a retinue of followers, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one does not crave service and attendance, nor manages the assembly with a mind of attachment.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, is indolent and lazy, indulging in the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of reclining, or the pleasure of leaning, at improper times or in excessive measure, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if one is afflicted by illness;
or if one lacks physical strength due to the exhaustion of traveling on a journey.
If one generates the desire to abandon that [fault], all details should be understood as previously explained.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*), engages in worldly talk with a mind of attachment and thus wastes time, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation.
If one wastes time through forgetfulness, this is called an offense and a transgression, though it is not an afflicted offense.
There is no offense in the following case:
seeing others engaged in conversation, one listens for a brief moment while remaining established in right mindfulness in order to protect their feelings.
If the matter is extraordinary, or if one briefly questions another, or answers another’s question, there is no offense.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, desires to settle the mind and stabilize it, yet out of resentment or being sustained by pride, fails to go to a teacher to request instruction, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted offense.
If one fails to request [teachings] due to indolence or laziness, it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if one encounters illness;
If one lacks physical strength;
or if one knows that the teacher’s instruction is erroneous;
or if one has heard much oneself and possesses the intellectual power capable of stabilizing the mind.
If one has already received the necessary instruction but does not request further guidance, there is no transgression.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, gives rise to the hindrance of sensual desire and tolerates it without relinquishing it, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled offense.
There is no transgression if:
one has generated the desire to abandon that [fault] and exerts diligent effort, yet because the afflictions are so intense and sharp that they overwhelm the mind, it manifests from time to time.
Just as it is with the hindrance of sensual desire, so it should be understood for the hindrances of ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, craves the flavor of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and perceives such craving for its flavor as a merit, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted offense.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if one generates the desire to sever those [faults], as explained in detail previously;
or if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, gives rise to such a view and establishes such a doctrine:
A bodhisattva should not listen to the teachings associated with the Śrāvaka vehicle;
should not uphold them;
and should not train in them.
Why would a bodhisattva employ the teachings corresponding to the Śrāvaka vehicle to hear, receive, uphold, and diligently practice them?
This is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva applies themselves with diligent study even to the treatises of non-Buddhists, let alone to the words of the Buddha.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
This was said in order to cause those who are exclusively devoted to the Hīnayāna teachings to abandon that desire.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, has not yet thoroughly studied the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, and having completely abandoned the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, devotes himself solely to training in the Śrāvakapiṭaka, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a non-afflicted violation.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, fails to engage in thorough study of the Buddha’s teachings when they are currently available, and instead applies themselves diligently to the treatises of non-Buddhist paths and various external doctrines, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
There is no transgression if one is of superior intelligence;
or if one is able to receive [the teaching] quickly.
If one is able to avoid forgetting over a long period of time;
if one is able to contemplate and penetrate its meaning;

and if, through investigating the Buddha’s teaching according to reason, one achieves a stable awareness that functions in tandem with it—then, if one constantly devotes two parts of each day to training in the Buddha’s words and one part to external studies, there is no transgression.

If a bodhisattva, dwelling securely in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline (*śīla-vinaya*), transgresses the bodhisattva dharma by seeking skillfulness in the treatises of heterodox paths and various non-Buddhist doctrines, cherishing them with a deep-seated mind, finding pleasure in them, and becoming addicted to their flavor—rather than approaching them as one would bitter medicine—this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation.

If a bodhisattva, while dwelling in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, hears the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and fails to give rise to faith and understanding regarding its profound points, its most supreme and profound true meaning of the Dharma, and the inconceivable spiritual powers of the Buddhas and bodhisattvas;

and if they instead harbor aversion, turn away from it, or disparage it—claiming that it does not lead to the goal, does not lead to the Dharma, was not spoken by the Tathāgata, and cannot benefit or bring happiness to sentient beings—this is called an offense, a transgression, and is a defiled violation.
Such slander may arise either from improper mental attention within oneself,
or from speaking thus in conformity with others.
If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, hear of the profound and most profound points and their minds do not believe or understand them.

At that time, the bodhisattva should accept it with firm faith, should be free from deceit and crookedness, and should train thus: "I have acted unskillfully; being blind and lacking the eye of wisdom, I have slandered the intentional language of the Tathāgatas as it was proclaimed by the eye of the Tathāgata."

In this way, the bodhisattva, acknowledging his own lack of knowledge, looks up to and defers to the Tathāgata, who possesses direct and manifest knowledge of all Buddha-dharmas and perceives them with equal clarity; practicing in such a manner, he commits no transgression.
Although they lack faith and understanding, they do not slander [the teachings].

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, possesses a mind of attachment toward others or a mind of malice, and thus praises themselves and disparages others, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases:
if it is for the purpose of subduing various evil non-Buddhists;
or if it is for the purpose of upholding the holy teaching of the Tathāgata.
If it is for the purpose of skillfully training or subduing them—as explained in detail previously;
or if one wishes to cause those who have not yet developed pure faith to do so, and to cause those who already possess pure faith to increase it further.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline, hears the preaching of the true Dharma or the analytical determination of its meaning, yet—restrained by pride and harboring a mind of resentment or a mind of malice—does not go to listen, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted offense.
If one fails to go and listen because of being obscured by indolence or laziness, it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one does not perceive [the opportunity].
If one has an illness;
if one lacks physical strength;
or if one knows that [the teaching] is being explained erroneously;
If it is for the sake of protecting the mind of that Dharma-preacher;
or if one correctly understands the meaning of what is being taught, having heard it repeatedly, retained it, and comprehended it;
or if one has already heard much, is fully endowed with hearing and retention, and has accumulated what has been heard.
If one wishes to dwell the mind uninterruptedly upon an object;
or if one strives to induce the superior meditative concentrations of a bodhisattva;

or if one recognizes for oneself that one is of the highest degree of dullness and obtuseness, such that one's wisdom is dull and turbid, making it difficult to receive and retain the teachings heard, and difficult to collect the mind upon an object of focus to bring it to concentration;
If one does not go to listen, there is no transgression in any case.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, intentionally disparages or treats with contempt a Dharma teacher; fails to show deep respect; mocks or ridicules them; and relies solely on the literal letter rather than the meaning—this is called an offense, a transgression, and it is a defiled violation.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, harbors a mind of resentment or a mind of malice toward sentient beings regarding tasks that ought to be performed for them, and thus fails to act as their companion.
That is to say: regarding the performance of tasks that ought to be done; or while traveling on a road, whether going or returning;
or regarding the application of effort in correctly explaining activities;
or regarding the protection and preservation of all wealth and treasures.
Whether it be during times of reconciliation or estrangement, dispute or litigation;
or during auspicious gatherings;
or during the performance of meritorious deeds;
If one does not act as a companion, it is called an offense, a transgression; this is an afflicted violation.
If one fails to act as a companion because of being obscured by laziness and indolence, it is a non-afflicted violation.
There is no transgression if one has an illness,
or if one lacks physical strength.
If one knows that the person can accomplish it for themselves;
if one knows that the petitioner already has their own support;
or if one knows that what is being done would lead to what is non-beneficial or what is contrary to the Dharma.
If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them, as explained in detail previously;
or if one has previously consented to act as an assistant for another;
or if one requests the assistance of another who possesses power;
If one is diligently cultivating wholesome qualities and does not wish to abandon them even for a moment;
if one is by nature dull-witted such that it is difficult to receive and retain the teachings heard, as explained extensively before;
or if it is for the sake of protecting the minds of many sentient beings.
If one protects the monastic regulations and does not act as an attendant, there is no transgression in either case.

However, if a bodhisattva, dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, sees sentient beings afflicted by a grave illness and, out of a mind of resentment or a mind of malice, fails to go and attend to them, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
If one fails to go and provide service because of being obscured by laziness or indolence,
it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one is personally ill;
If one lacks the strength;
or if one requests another who is capable and compliant to go and attend to them;
or if one knows that the patient has someone to rely upon and protect them.
If one knows that the patient has the strength to attend to their own needs;
if one understands that they are capable of sustaining themselves despite being afflicted by a chronic illness;
or if it is for the sake of diligently cultivating vast, unsurpassed, and sublime wholesome qualities; [then one should not provide service].
If one wishes to protect and maintain the wholesome qualities one has cultivated so that they remain uninterrupted;

or if one knows oneself to be of superior dullness and stupidity, such that one’s wisdom is blunt and turbid, making it difficult to receive and retain the teachings heard, and difficult to collect the mind upon an object of focus to bring it to concentration;
or if one has previously promised others to perform services for them.
Just as one acts toward a sick person, so should it be understood that one acts toward those who suffer, desiring to become their companion in order to eliminate their suffering.

If a bodhisattva, dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline (*śīla-vinaya*), sees sentient beings extensively practicing what is unreasonable for the sake of matters pertaining to the present life or future lives, yet—with a mind of resentment or a mind of malice—does not explain the correct principle as it truly is, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.
If one fails to provide the teaching due to being shrouded by indolence or laziness, it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one is personally ignorant;
If one lacks the strength;
or if one requests another who possesses strength to speak;
or if that person themselves possesses the power of wisdom;
If they are already being sustained by other virtuous friends;
if one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them, as explained in detail previously;
or if one knows that when explaining the true and correct principle, they will give rise to a mind of resentment or utter malicious words; [in these cases, one should not speak].
There is no transgression if the teaching is not proclaimed because the recipient holds perverted views, lacks love and respect, or if one knows that the person's nature is corrupt and stubborn.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, fails to recognize the kindness of sentient beings who have previously bestowed favors upon them, fails to understand that kindness, and harbors a mind of resentment such that they are unwilling to repay it appropriately in their presence, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation.
If one fails to provide recompense due to being obscured by indolence or laziness, it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression in cases where,
despite applying diligent effort, one is unable to provide recompense due to a lack of power or ability.

If one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them—as explained in detail previously—or if one wishes to repay their kindness but they do not accept it, there is no transgression in either case.

However, if a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, sees sentient beings fallen into circumstances where they have lost their wealth, kin, or status, and are beset by much grief and distress, yet out of a mind of resentment fails to go and offer consolation, this is called an offense; it is a transgression and constitutes a defiled violation.
If one fails to go and provide explanation and resolution because of being shrouded by indolence or laziness,
it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression in cases where, as previously understood, one does not act as an assistant for the affairs of others.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, possesses food, drink, and other requisites for livelihood, and upon seeing a seeker arrive seeking such things as food and drink, fails to give them out of a mind of resentment or a mind of anger and vexation, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation.
If one fails to give due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one currently lacks any material wealth to give;
If they seek things that are not in accordance with the Dharma or things that are unsuitable;
or if one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them, as explained in detail previously;
or if the seeker is someone whom the king would disapprove of, and one thus protects the king’s sentiments; [in these cases, there is no offense].
If one upholds the monastic regulations and does not bestow gifts, there is no transgression in either case.

If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, gathers a circle of disciples but, out of a mind of resentment, fails to provide them with timely, unerring instruction and unerring admonition; [this constitutes a transgression].

If one knows that the assembly is in need, yet for the sake of those who possess pure faith—such as householders, lay devotees, or brahmins—one does not seek in accordance with the Dharma clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, medicinal requisites for illness, or other articles for the support of the body, and fails to provide them at the appropriate time, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is a defiled violation.

If one fails to go to provide instruction, fails to go to provide admonition, and fails to seek out requisites in accordance with the Dharma due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, it is an unafflicted transgression.
There is no offense if one intends to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue that person, as explained in detail previously;
or if one is upholding the regulations of the Sangha.
If one has an illness;
or if one lacks the physical strength to engage in the practice;
or if one requests another who possesses such strength to act on their behalf;
If one knows that the assembly is widely renowned in the world for possessing great merit, such that each member has the power to seek out their own requisites for the body, such as clothing;
or if one has already provided instruction and admonition to each according to what is appropriate, doing so without error;
or if one knows that among the assembly there are former non-Buddhists who have entered for the sake of stealing the Dharma and are incapable of being tamed—there is no offense in these cases.

If a bodhisattva, dwelling in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, harbors a mind of resentment and does not comply with the wishes of other sentient beings, this is called an offense, a transgression; it is an afflicted violation.
If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, one does not comply with their request,
it is a non-afflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if what they desire is not suitable for them;
If one has an illness;
if one lacks the physical strength to engage in formal practice;
or if one is observing the regulations of the Saṃgha.
If that which is beloved by them is suitable for them, yet is neither suitable nor beloved for the majority;
or if it is for the purpose of subduing various evil non-Buddhists;
or if one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline and subdue them—as explained in detail previously; [in such cases, it is not a transgression].
There is no transgression in cases where [the mind] does not follow one's own inclination.
If a bodhisattva, while abiding in the code of bodhisattva ethical discipline, harbors a mind of resentment and is unwilling to proclaim the actual virtues of others,
or unwilling to praise their actual reputation;
If he does not praise a truly excellent teaching by saying "Well said," it is called an offense, a transgression, and is a defiled violation.
If it is due to indolence, laziness, or negligence that he fails to proclaim it and so forth, it is a non-defiled violation.
There is no transgression if one knows that the person’s nature is to have few desires and acts thus to protect their feelings;
or if the person is ill.
If one lacks the physical strength;
if one wishes to employ skillful means to discipline or subdue them, as explained in detail previously;
or if it is to protect the regulations of the Saṃgha;
If one knows that through such causes as public praise and so forth, those afflictions as pride and agitation arise which are meaningless;
and if, in order to prevent this fault, one knows that although those qualities appear to be virtues, they are not actual virtues;
and if one knows that although that reputation appears to be a good reputation, it is not an actual reputation;
There is no transgression if one knows that although the other's speech appears to be excellent, it is in fact not so;
or if it is for the purpose of subduing various evil non-Buddhists;
or if it is to bring another's discourse to its conclusion, rather than proclaiming one's own views, and so forth.

If bodhisattvas, while abiding in the bodhisattva’s code of pure ethical discipline, see sentient beings who ought to be rebuked, ought to be punished, or ought to be expelled, yet—with a defiled mind—do not rebuke them;
or although they rebuke them, do not punish them or provide them with instruction according to the Dharma;
or although they punish them and provide them with instruction according to the Dharma, do not expel them: this is called an offense, a transgression, and is a defiled violation.
If, due to indolence, laziness, or negligence, one fails to reprimand [the offender] up to and including expelling them,
it is an unafflicted transgression.
There is no transgression if one understands that the person is incurable, unfit for conversation, prone to uttering coarse words, and full of resentment, and thus should be abandoned.
If one considers the time;
if one considers that because of this there will be quarrels, disputes, and contention;
or if one considers that because of this the Saṃgha will become noisy and distracted.
If it causes the Saṃgha to be divided;
and if one knows that those sentient beings do not harbor deceit or crookedness, but have achieved a superior and intense sense of shame and dread of blame, and will quickly return to purity;
then, to neither reprimand them nor even expel them constitutes no transgression whatsoever.

If a bodhisattva, dwelling securely in the bodhisattva’s code of ethical discipline (*śīla-vinaya*), possesses and has fully accomplished various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the majesty of miraculous manifestations, such that they are able to terrify those sentient beings who should be terrified and able to attract and gather those who should be attracted and gathered;

yet, for the sake of avoiding offerings of faith, does not manifest supernormal powers to terrify or attract them—this is called an offense, a transgression, though it is not an afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) violation.
There is no transgression in the following cases:

if one knows that the sentient beings therein are mostly attached to perverse fixations, are evil non-Buddhists, revile the noble ones, and have established wrong views, then there is no transgression in not manifesting supernormal powers to terrify or attract them.
Furthermore, there is no transgression in any case where:
the mind is excessively deranged;
or one is oppressed by intense physical suffering.
If one has never previously received the pure vows of ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*),
it should be known that there is no transgression whatsoever.
However, if a bodhisattva, having correctly received the vows of ethical discipline from another, possesses a well-purified intention for training and an intention for enlightenment;

With the intention to benefit all sentient beings, one should give rise to the utmost reverence and respect; from the very beginning, one should apply oneself with diligence and not commit any transgression.
Should a transgression occur, one must immediately repent and eliminate it according to the Dharma, so as to restore purity.

In this way, one should know that all transgressions of a bodhisattva are subsumed under *duṣkṛta* (misdeeds); these should be confessed and extinguished before those who are capable—persons of the Hīnayāna or Mahāyāna who are able to understand and accept the meaning expressed through speech.

If a bodhisattva violates any of the aforementioned *pārājika* dharmas through an intense degree of mental affliction (*paryavasthāna*), they lose the ethical discipline (*śīla-saṃvara*) and must receive it again.

If they violate any of the aforementioned *pārājika* dharmas through a middling degree of mental affliction, they should, before three persons or more, perform the rite for the disclosure and removal of evil deeds (*pratikarman*). First, they should state the name of the offense committed and speak as follows:

"Venerable one" (or "Great Virtue"), I, who am named so-and-so, have transgressed the Bodhisattva Vinaya rules; regarding the matter just mentioned, I have committed an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*)."
The remainder is as in the method for confessing and extinguishing *dukkaṭa* offenses for a bhikṣu; it should be explained in this way.

If one commits an offense against the aforementioned *pārājika* dharmas or other violations due to minor entanglements (*mṛdu-paryavasthāna*), the method for confessing before a single person (*pudgala*) should be understood to be as previously described.

If there is no person to whom one may confess and thereby eliminate the transgression, the bodhisattva, with a pure intention, gives rise to a self-vow, thinking: "I shall certainly guard myself against the future and never commit it again."
In this way, one emerges from and becomes purified of transgressions.

Furthermore, regarding these various matters of transgression concerning the bodhisattva training rules (*śikṣāpada*), the Buddha taught them scattered throughout various *sūtras* according to the needs of his disciples—namely, the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*). Now, they are compiled and explained here in this *mātṛkā* of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
In this regard, a bodhisattva should give rise to reverence, abide in the utmost respect, and apply themselves with focused diligence to cultivation and study.
*Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, one fascicle.
